paper_style.palette_strategy: The two method diagrams use local raster palettes: Figure 1 uses pastel blue/orange/yellow/red/green semantic roles and Figure 2 uses red/green error-versus-acceptance cues on neutral panels. All nine tables are monochrome vector objects with black text/rules on white. No method color role is shared across figures and tables.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Body text, mathematical notation, table text and rules are vector PDF objects. Figure 1 is a 1926×812 RGB raster XObject placed at about 438 ppi; Figure 2 is a 1126×832 RGB raster XObject placed at about 409 ppi. No paper-specific public plot/table/LaTeX source was found for either figure or any table.
paper_style.style_consistency: The paper uses a consistent serif caption/body and rule system, with PDF-object table text ranging from about 6.67 pt in dense diagnostic tables to about 8.67 pt in compact tables. The two embedded diagrams introduce distinct raster sans/monospace-like labels and local colors; appendix tables reuse the main diagnostic header grammar but remain highly compressed.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: RefineStat workflow: (1) A user provides data and prompt to the language model, which generates a probabilistic program. (2) Constrained semantic decoding enforces syntactic and semantic validity of the generated program. (3) A Bayesian reliability check diagnoses convergence, divergences, and predictive validity. If failures are detected, the model is refined by backtracking and re-sampling priors or likelihoods. (4) Upon passing checks, we get final reliable probabilistic program.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue outlines and pale-blue fills mark constrained semantic generation; peach and orange mark the Bayesian reliability check; yellow labels identify prior and likelihood fragments; red X and green check encode failed versus accepted refinement; gray/white boxes carry code, data and prompt content. Labels, box shapes and arrows add partial redundancy, but the state palette remains important.

encodings.x: Left-to-right workflow from data/prompt through semantic generation and reliability checking to the final reliable model
encodings.y: Vertical placement separates inputs, generated prior/likelihood fragments, refinement loop and accepted output
encodings.color: Local pastel role/state colors distinguish generation, reliability checking, prior/likelihood labels, failure and acceptance
encodings.shape: Rounded process boxes, dotted code-fragment boxes, arrows, red cross and green check icons
encodings.line: Solid directional arrows and a black return/refinement path encode control flow
encodings.text: Direct labels name six semantic predicates, Bayesian checks, prior/likelihood fragments, process steps and final output

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual method interface rather than a quantitative sample. The raster diagram shows data plus prompt entering an LM, six validation predicates, prior and likelihood code fragments, Bayesian checks for R-hat, ESS, sampler health, convergence, divergences and predictive validity, a failed refinement branch, and a final reliable statistical model. No observations, denominator, estimate or uncertainty interval is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 3 introduces the workflow; Definitions 2–4 and the six predicates in Section 3.1 formalize the semantic and statistical gates; Algorithm 1 implements constrained decoding and guided refinement. The figure is structural evidence for the method-interface claim and motivates the run-rate, diagnostic and ablation tables, not a performance estimate.
design_strengths: The four numbered stages expose the complete path from user input to semantic filtering, reliability diagnosis and an accepted model.
A local predicate/check vocabulary and direct labels let the reader map the diagram to the formal definitions without a separate global legend.
Arrows, dotted code boxes, a red failure cross and a green acceptance check make the refinement loop and terminal state visible.
design_weaknesses: The embedded raster is dense: predicate labels, code snippets and diagnostic names are small at the placed size despite the high native resolution.
Blue/orange/yellow/red/green state semantics are only partly duplicated by shape or line treatment, so grayscale reproduction weakens the distinction.
The diagram mixes serif, sans-serif and code-like text styles that do not expose a reproducible source font specification.
The caption describes the process but does not define the thresholds, iteration limit or quantitative reliability score; no uncertainty or cost is visualized.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use one labeled process schematic to connect input, constrained generation, diagnostic gate, failure-driven refinement and accepted output; duplicate any state color with labels, shapes or line semantics for accessible reproduction.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Constrained decoding in RefineStat fixing a TypeError from using sd instead of sigma, as illustrated in Section 1.

family: monospace-like raster code and prompt text

color.semantic_mapping: Red text and cross marks identify the invalid sd parameter/error branch; green check marks identify predicates that pass; pale gray/white panels carry the prompt, code fragments and language-model block. Color is supported by direct predicate labels and cross/check glyphs, but red/green still carries status.

encodings.x: Generation and validation progress from prompt and language model to code fragment and predicate checks
encodings.y: Vertical arrangement separates prompt, generated prefix, invalid candidate, corrected candidate and upward resampling path
encodings.color: Red denotes the sd/TypeError rejection; green denotes predicate acceptance; neutral fills distinguish prompt/code panels
encodings.shape: Prompt and code rectangles, rounded language-model block, arrows, green checks and red cross
encodings.line: Thin solid arrows connect generation and the two candidate validation paths
encodings.text: Monospaced code, prompt text and direct labels for k-th step and predicates phi_1, phi_2 and phi_3

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative code-generation example, not a numerical plot. A PyMC prompt and partial generated program lead to an invalid Normal call using sd=10; constrained decoding rejects it and accepts sigma=10 after the semantic checks. No sample count, metric, denominator or uncertainty is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 1 motivates the sd-to-sigma TypeError; Section 3.1 defines parameter validity and the other semantic predicates; the figure gives a concrete local rejection path before the broader Bayesian diagnostics. It supports interpretability of constrained decoding rather than a quantitative result.
design_strengths: The invalid and corrected code fragments are shown side by side with predicate checks, making the parameter-validity mechanism concrete.
A compact prompt-to-LM-to-candidate flow connects the formal phi predicates to a recognizable PyMC example.
Direct code labels and check/cross glyphs reduce the need for a legend and preserve the local sequence of rejection and acceptance.
design_weaknesses: The inset is small and rasterized; long prompt/code lines and predicate labels are difficult to inspect at normal reading scale.
The red/green status palette is not grayscale-safe and is not supplemented by distinct line styles or textures.
Only one TypeError example is shown, so the diagram does not communicate distribution, dependency, support or type failures equally.
The caption names the correction but omits the exact predicate semantics and does not show a downstream sampling or reliability outcome.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair an invalid and corrected code fragment with direct semantic-gate labels and check/cross marks; show the full prompt-to-validation path while keeping the example short enough for an inset.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Run rates for Standard, Syncode, and RefineStat by temperature

tables.uncertainty: None is displayed. Each cell is a point run-rate value; no replicate count, dispersion or interval is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three temperatures (0.2, 0.3, 0.4) cross Standard, Syncode and RefineStat. Run rate is the fraction of programs that successfully produce posterior samples; values are decimals (0.10–0.50), but the table gives no denominator or number of generated programs. RefineStat values are bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.1 defines run rate and attributes failures to numerical, sampling, warning and static-compilation causes. This is the first quantitative test of the semantic-validation workflow in Figure 1 and supports the claim that RefineStat improves executable-program reliability across temperatures.
design_strengths: A compact single-level header makes the three temperature conditions and method comparison immediately scannable.
Bold proposal values direct attention to the claimed improvement without adding a separate legend.
Booktabs rules and generous row spacing keep the small four-column object legible.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits the run denominator, workload and aggregation procedure, so the decimals cannot be independently interpreted from the table alone.
Point estimates hide variation across prompts/seeds and do not expose the individual failure categories discussed in surrounding prose.
Method naming is not visually normalized with the small-caps rendering used elsewhere in the paper.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a short condition-by-method run-rate table for a first reliability headline, but state the denominator and replicate design in the caption and report uncertainty or failure counts when stochastic generation is central.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Comparison of Diagnostic Scores and ELPD-LOO for Standard vs. RefineStat

tables.uncertainty: Mean and Std are printed for every diagnostic/ELPD group; repeated baseline selection and RefineStat comparisons are described as five repetitions in Section 5.2. A ✗ denotes that no valid program was produced. No confidence intervals are shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five datasets (8 Schools, Dugongs, Peregrine, Surgical and GP) are grouped by dataset; each has four model/variant rows, giving 40 rows. The 15 columns are Dataset, Model, Variant, then six metric groups (Reliability Score, split-R-hat, ESS Bulk, Divergences, Pareto k and ELPD LOO), each with Mean and Std. The prose says five representative metrics, but the visible table contains six groups. Bold cells mark RefineStat wins or emphasized ELPD-LOO differences; ✗ encodes an invalid/no-result run.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.2 compares best-of-five Standard baseline runs with a single RefineStat run under identical prompts, then repeats the process five times. The table is the main diagnostic-quality evidence behind the reliability claim, showing why a slightly lower ELPD can be preferred when convergence and divergence diagnostics are sound.
design_strengths: Two header levels keep six diagnostic families aligned with paired Mean/Std subcolumns.
Dataset grouping and Variant rows support within-model baseline/refinement comparisons, while bold cells foreground the paper’s decision rule.
The explicit ✗ state preserves failed exploration rather than silently dropping missing programs.
design_weaknesses: Fifteen columns at approximately 6.67 pt are difficult to read and require substantial cross-row tracking.
The table caption does not define metric thresholds, five-run aggregation, model conditions or the meaning of the bolding rule; those details are only in prose.
The prose/table mismatch (“five” metrics versus six visible metric groups) weakens auditability, and no denominator accompanies failed ✗ rows.
Mean/Std text is the only variability encoding; no visual distinction separates diagnostics with different units/scales.
tables.reusable_pattern: For multi-dataset diagnostic comparisons, use grouped dataset blocks and paired Mean/Std columns with an explicit failure glyph; reserve this width for a compact appendix or add a stronger header/caption contract that defines every metric and replicate.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Comparison of ELPD LOO scores with BoxLM (Li et al., 2024), RefineStat using DQ-7B, and Expert values

tables.uncertainty: RefineStat/DQ-7B and OpenAI-o3 report mean ± std; Expert and BoxLM are single values without dispersion. The caption does not specify a confidence interval or the number of runs.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five datasets (Eight schools, Dugongs, Peregrine, Surgical and GP) are rows. Columns compare Expert, RefineStat with DQ-7B (mean ± std), BoxLM with GPT-4, and OpenAI-o3 (mean ± std) using ELPD LOO. The GP BoxLM cell is an em dash because that dataset is outside BoxLM’s evaluation suite. DQ-7B values are averaged over five runs according to adjacent prose.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.3 positions this table as an external quality comparison. It extends the internal Standard/RefineStat diagnostics in Table 2 to Expert programs, BoxLM and OpenAI o3, supporting the claim that RefineStat is comparable to or better than strong baselines on selected datasets.
design_strengths: Five columns fit the external comparison in one compact surface and keep the single missing GP comparison explicit.
Mean ± std is embedded in method headers/cells, making stochastic versus single-reference columns distinguishable.
The ELPD direction is consistent across rows and the dataset names are easy to scan.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not state that RefineStat and o3 use different run aggregation or that Expert/BoxLM lack uncertainty.
Negative ELPD values and mixed dataset scales make raw cross-row ranking hard without contextual bounds.
No bold/best marker or explicit decision annotation indicates which differences support the headline, so the reader must rely on surrounding prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a narrow external-baseline table when one scalar estimand is the comparison target, preserving missing coverage with an explicit dash and labeling which columns are repeated-run means rather than single references.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Ablation Study: Impact of Semantic Validation Checks on Run rate

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or replicate dispersion is printed. ΔRun is a point difference in percentage points relative to the all-components row.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five rows compare RefineStat with all components (50.0%) against four leave-one-component-out variants: parameter validity (35.5%, −14.5), distribution validity (26.5%, −9), parse-ability (21.0%, −5.5) and grammar-guided generation (11.0%, −10.0%). Run % is compilation/run success; adjacent Section 5.4 states the analysis spans all models and ten random seeds.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.4 uses this table to attribute run-rate changes to semantic predicates and to argue that parameter validity is especially critical. It is the direct mechanism ablation supporting the semantic-gating blocks in Figures 1 and 2.
design_strengths: The all-components reference row and ΔRun column make the ablation contrast immediately interpretable.
One row per predicate maps directly to the formal validation-predicate list and the method diagram.
Percentage formatting preserves the practical scale of the compilation/run-rate change.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not identify the ten-seed/all-model design or define whether Run % means compilation, execution or both; those distinctions are in surrounding prose.
No standard deviation or per-model breakdown shows whether component effects are stable across models.
The grammar-guided-generation row is an implementation component not included in the three “essential” predicates named earlier, which the table does not explain.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair a complete-system row with one leave-one-component-out row per mechanism and a delta column; state the unit, replicate structure and whether effects are averaged across models directly in the caption.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Run-rate comparison when using NumPyro as the inference backend.

tables.uncertainty: None is displayed; the three temperature-by-method values are point run rates with no denominator or dispersion.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three temperatures compare Standard and RefineStat under NumPyro: 0.17 vs 0.34, 0.15 vs 0.35 and 0.15 vs 0.33. The values are fractions of programs that compile/execute according to the surrounding Section 5.5 text; the Qwen-2.5-Coder–7B model and prompting setup are not repeated in the table.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.5 presents Table 5 as backend-generalization evidence and compares it with the PyMC3 run rates in Table 1. It tests whether the semantic filtering/refinement interface carries beyond the primary PPL implementation.
design_strengths: The matched temperature rows make the backend comparison easy to read against Table 1.
The small table keeps the generalizability check subordinate to the main results while retaining exact values.
Bold RefineStat cells create a consistent proposal emphasis with Table 1.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits the Qwen model, prompting condition, workload and denominator, preventing standalone interpretation.
There is no variability or per-dataset evidence here; the table only supports a coarse run-rate claim.
The table label uses “NumPyro” while surrounding prose alternates between “PyMC3 experiment” and backend names, with no explicit unit note.
tables.reusable_pattern: Reuse the primary run-rate table’s condition-by-method layout for a backend replication, but put model, workload and denominator in the caption so the small robustness object remains independently auditable.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Diagnostics and ELPD-LOO results for NumPyro using Qwen-2.5-Coder–7B, demonstrating the generalizability of RefineStat.

tables.uncertainty: Mean and Std are shown for six metric groups across the Standard/RefineStat rows; a ✗ marks no valid program. The table has no confidence intervals or explicit run count; aggregation is inherited from the Table 2/Section 5.2 protocol.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five dataset groups (8 Schools, Dugongs, Peregrine, Surgical and GP) each contain Standard and RefineStat rows, for 10 rows. There are 14 columns: Dataset, Variant, and six metric groups—Reliability Score, R-hat, ESS Bulk, Divergences, Pareto k and ELPD LOO—each with Mean and Std. The GP Standard row is all ✗ while RefineStat has numerical diagnostics.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 5.5 says Table 6 repeats the Table 2 diagnostics for NumPyro and Qwen-2.5-Coder–7B. It is the diagnostic counterpart to Table 5 and supports the claim that semantic filtering and guided refinement generalize beyond PyMC.
design_strengths: The two-level Mean/Std header mirrors Table 2, enabling a direct diagnostic-system comparison across backends.
Dataset blocks and explicit failed-program glyphs retain the robustness boundary instead of hiding unsupported cases.
The table keeps the backend/model condition in the caption while preserving the same metric vocabulary as the main diagnostic table.
design_weaknesses: Approximately 6.67 pt body text and 14 columns make exact values hard to inspect, especially for the long Pareto-k and ELPD columns.
The caption does not repeat the replicate count or explain the failure denominator, and no visual emphasis marks the most important cross-backend differences.
The table is adjacent to Table 5 but the pair lacks a shared subheading or visual grouping that would make the robustness package explicit.
tables.reusable_pattern: Mirror a main diagnostic table for a second backend with identical metric order and explicit failure rows; keep the header contract and replicate design unchanged so readers can compare without relearning the encoding.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Semantic filtering of LLM-proposed likelihoods.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: this is a qualitative code-path table with no estimated quantity or repeated-run statistic.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three likelihood proposals are printed as monospaced code: a hallucinated pm.ExtNormal rejected by distribution validity; pm.Normal using deprecated sd rejected by parameter validity; and pm.Normal using sigma accepted by all checks. Outcome text and code fragments, not numeric data, carry the evidence.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix C.1 uses this table to instantiate the semantic-filtering stage before NUTS diagnostics and guided resampling. It concretizes the distribution/parameter-validity predicates that Figures 1 and 2 summarize and bridges them to the later diagnostic example.
design_strengths: The Proposal–Check–Outcome columns align the candidate code, responsible predicate and decision in a compact causal table.
Monospaced proposal cells preserve exact API spelling, while bold outcome words make accept/reject status visible.
The three rows cover both a hallucinated distribution and a deprecated parameter before showing the accepted form.
design_weaknesses: Long code wraps across several lines, and the proposal column is small enough that syntax differences require close inspection.
The caption does not say that the examples are illustrative rather than a frequency summary, nor does it define the PPL/library version.
Color is absent and outcome emphasis is typographic only; the table does not visually connect the accepted row to a downstream diagnostic result.
tables.reusable_pattern: Show exact candidate code beside the semantic predicate and decision outcome when a method claim hinges on executable validity; keep the rows representative and label them as examples rather than empirical frequencies.

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8: Comparison of Itergen, Baseline, and RefineStat Variants with Multipliers.

tables.uncertainty: Mean and Std are reported for token counts over five runs according to Appendix G.1. The final Token Ratio is a point multiplier; the Average Token Ratio summary is 1.9x and has no interval.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five dataset rows compare Itergen, Baseline, RefineStat without the refinement loop, and RefineStat, with Mean and Std token counts for each method and a final Token Ratio column. A sixth summary row reports Average Token Ratio = 1.9x. Ratios range from 0.6x (Dugongs) to 2.5x (Eight Schools and GP), making the cost/early-convergence trade-off explicit.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix G.1 uses this table to quantify the token overhead of semantic refinement and explain why RefineStat is often about twice the baseline cost. It qualifies the reliability gains in Tables 1–6 with an efficiency boundary and separates no-refinement behavior from the full method.
design_strengths: Grouped Mean/Std columns preserve the cost distribution for each method rather than reporting only a multiplier.
The Token Ratio column and final average row provide a fast summary of the resource trade-off.
Dataset rows expose heterogeneous overhead, including the under-one multiplier case, instead of presenting only an aggregate.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not state the five-run design, tokenization/model configuration or whether truncation/budget failures are included.
Ten columns and repeated Mean/Std labels are dense; the full-method column is visually emphasized but the ratio baseline is not restated in the header.
The bold summary emphasis does not distinguish statistically meaningful variability from formatting hierarchy.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair absolute resource means/dispersion with a baseline-normalized ratio and an aggregate row, while retaining per-dataset rows so cost overhead can be interpreted alongside quality gains.

tables.label: Table 9

caption.text: Table 9: Comparison of Diagnostic Scores and ELPD-LOO for RefineStat variants.

tables.uncertainty: Mean and Std are printed for six diagnostic/ELPD groups; the surrounding Appendix G.2 text describes controlled prompt modifications but the table does not state an explicit run count or interval.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five dataset groups (Dugongs, Eight Schools, Peregrine, GP and Surgical) each contain four variants—RefineStat, anonymized prompt (AP), syntactic obfuscation (SO) and AP-SO—for 20 rows. The 14 columns are Dataset, Variant and six Mean/Std metric groups: Reliability Score, R-hat, ESS Bulk, Divergences, Pareto k and ELPD LOO. Values compare memorization-stress variants to the original method.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix G.2 uses Table 9 to test whether anonymizing metadata and changing numeric notation preserve reliability, convergence and predictive behavior. It is the paper’s direct memorization robustness evidence and complements the semantic ablation in Table 4 and backend replication in Table 6.
design_strengths: A fixed metric order and four-variant block make within-dataset stress-test comparisons possible.
The two-level Mean/Std header matches Table 2/Table 6, preserving a common diagnostic grammar across main and appendix results.
Dataset grouping exposes where obfuscation changes ELPD or diagnostics rather than hiding heterogeneity in one average.
design_weaknesses: The 14-column table is extremely dense at approximately 6.67 pt and spans a nearly full appendix page, slowing exact row tracking.
The caption does not define AP, SO or AP-SO; readers must use the preceding prose, and the table gives no explicit run count.
No bold/best marker or difference column summarizes deviations from original RefineStat, so the memorization conclusion requires manual comparisons across 20 rows.
The table reports dispersion textually but offers no visual encoding for the magnitude of changes or failures.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use matched stress-test variant blocks with unchanged metric columns to audit memorization or prompt sensitivity; add compact delta columns or caption-defined abbreviations when the row count makes manual comparison prohibitive.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes the RefineStat pipeline from prompt/data through semantic validity, Bayesian reliability checks, refinement and a reliable model. Figure 2 grounds one parameter-validity rejection in a concrete PyMC code path. Tables 1–3 carry run-rate, diagnostic and external predictive comparisons; Table 4 isolates semantic components; Tables 5–6 test NumPyro generalization; Appendix Tables 7–9 provide code-level semantic examples, token-cost trade-offs and memorization stress tests. Algorithm 1 is a procedural block rather than a Figure/Table and is intentionally excluded from the arrays.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All objects use a regular serif “Figure/Table n:” caption with a descriptive title. Figure 1 lists four workflow stages, Figure 2 names the TypeError example, and Tables 1–9 mostly state the comparison target without a numerical conclusion. Captions generally omit denominators, seed/run counts, threshold definitions and abbreviation expansions, leaving those details to nearby prose.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Compact tables use one-level condition/method headers; dense diagnostic and token tables use two levels with paired Mean/Std subcolumns. Up/down arrows encode metric direction, Dataset/Model/Variant columns define grouping, and ✗ preserves failed generation. The visible Table 2 has six metric groups although the surrounding prose calls them five representative metrics; units and denominator contracts are not consistently in headers or captions.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 1 maps the formal semantic predicates and Bayesian reliability score to an executable pipeline; Figure 2 instantiates parameter validity. Tables 1–3 quantify reliability, diagnostics and external ELPD-LOO; Table 4 directly ablates validation components; Tables 5–6 replicate run-rate/diagnostic evidence on NumPyro; Table 7 gives semantic proposals; Table 8 measures refinement cost; Table 9 stress-tests prompt memorization.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main Figures 1–2 and Tables 1–6 cover method, primary PyMC results, external comparison, ablation and NumPyro generalization. Appendix Table 7 expands the semantic-filtering example from Section 3.1/C.1, Table 8 quantifies the token overhead discussed in G.1, and Table 9 tests anonymized/obfuscated prompts in G.2. No appendix figure is present in the PDF.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Serif body/captions and Computer Modern math establish the document baseline. Dense main Tables 2 and 6 and appendix Table 9 use approximately 6.67 pt body text, while Tables 1, 3–5, 7 and 8 are about 8.67 pt. Embedded raster diagrams use smaller heterogeneous labels and code-like type, so object-level legibility varies even though table structure is consistent.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Figure 1 uses blue/orange/yellow/red/green process roles and Figure 2 uses red/green semantic outcomes; tables use only black and white. Because no color palette persists into tables or across the two diagrams, method identity is carried by labels and row/column keys rather than a global color encoding. Figure 1 and Figure 2 are not grayscale-safe for their status classes.

most_reusable_patterns: A labeled process schematic that joins user input, constrained semantic generation, diagnostic gating, failure-driven refinement and an accepted output.
Grouped diagnostic tables with stable metric order, paired Mean/Std columns, explicit failed-program glyphs and dataset blocks.
Leave-one-component-out rows with a complete-system baseline and a delta column for mechanism attribution.
A cost table that pairs per-dataset mean/dispersion with a baseline-normalized token ratio, followed by matched stress-test variants.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1, because it is the clearest single interface for the semantic-plus-diagnostic refinement loop.
Table 2, because it carries the main reliability/convergence/predictive-quality evidence and preserves failed programs.
Table 4, because it most directly distinguishes which semantic checks drive run-rate gains.
Table 8 and Table 9, because they bound the reliability claim with token cost and memorization-stress behavior.
failure_patterns: The supplied automatic inventory labels an exact source but lists unrelated SQL Spider assets; PDF-first inspection finds no validated paper-specific visual or LaTeX source in the linked repository.
Dense diagnostic tables (about 6.67 pt, 14–15 columns) are difficult to audit, and captions omit run denominators, thresholds and replicate details.
Figures rely on local red/green or multi-color semantics with limited grayscale redundancy and heterogeneous raster typography.
Captions are mostly descriptive rather than self-contained findings; Table 2 also conflicts with nearby prose on the number of reported metrics.
Mean/Std text is repeated without compact deltas or visual uncertainty encodings, making 20-row variant comparisons and cross-dataset trade-offs laborious.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Use two compact colored raster schematics to explain semantic gating and diagnostic refinement, then use monochrome grouped Mean/Std tables for run-rate, quality, ablation and backend claims, with appendix tables extending the same grammar to semantic examples, token cost and memorization stress tests.
